tagline: Every case starts with a scene, moves to a verdict, and ends with a defence.

levels.name: The Scene
levels.goal: Name what happened, clearly and correctly.

levels.name: The Verdict
levels.goal: Talk about punishment and causes with natural collocations.

levels.name: The Defence
levels.goal: Argue with nuance: idioms, precise terms, hedging.

words.def: do something illegal
words.ex: Most people who commit a crime never expect to be caught.

words.def: a minor crime, such as shoplifting or pickpocketing
words.ex: There’s some petty crime in the bazaar, but it’s generally safe.

words.def: stealing goods from a shop
words.ex: The shop installed cameras after a wave of shoplifting.

words.def: stealing from someone’s pocket or bag
words.ex: Keep your bag in front of you — pickpockets love the metro.

words.def: damaging public or private property on purpose
words.ex: Graffiti on bus stops is a common form of vandalism.

words.def: breaking into a building, usually a home, to steal
words.ex: Our neighbours were burgled while they were on holiday.

words.def: taking something from a person or place using force or threats
words.ex: Two men on a motorbike carried out the robbery in seconds.
words.note: you rob a person or a bank; you steal a thing

words.def: the general word for stealing
words.ex: Car theft has fallen thanks to better alarms.

words.def: tricking people in order to get money
words.ex: The fraudster pretended to be calling from the bank.

words.def: driving after drinking alcohol
words.ex: He lost his licence for drink-driving.

words.def: a person who sees a crime happen; to see it
words.ex: Several people witnessed the robbery.

words.def: when the police take someone to the station because they may have committed a crime
words.ex: He was arrested for shoplifting.

words.def: tell the police that a crime has happened
words.ex: We reported the theft the next morning.

words.def: the police and other agencies that make people obey the law
words.ex: My cousin works in law enforcement.

words.def: how much crime there is in a place
words.ex: The crime rate in our area is quite low.

words.def: an official record of the crimes a person has committed
words.ex: It’s hard to find work with a criminal record.

words.def: make people afraid to do something because of the possible punishment
words.ex: CCTV cameras act as a deterrent to thieves.

words.def: make someone decide not to do something
words.ex: Tough fines deter people from drink-driving.

words.w: be tough on crime / be soft on crime
words.def: punish crime strictly / not strictly enough
words.ex: Every politician promises to be tough on crime.

words.def: a very strict punishment / a light one
words.ex: Many felt the sentence was far too lenient.

words.def: spend time in prison as a punishment
words.ex: He served a ten-year sentence for fraud.

words.def: be officially found guilty by a court
words.ex: She was convicted of fraud and sentenced to three years.
words.note: accused = said to have done it · convicted = proven

words.def: a punishment that does not involve prison, e.g. community service or probation
words.ex: First-time offenders often get a non-custodial sentence.

words.def: unpaid work for the community as a punishment
words.ex: She was ordered to do 200 hours of community service.

words.def: commit a crime again after being punished
words.ex: Without job training, many ex-prisoners reoffend within a year.

words.def: start committing crimes, often because of difficult circumstances
words.ex: Poverty is one reason why young people turn to crime.

words.def: return to normal life after prison
words.ex: Ex-prisoners need support to reintegrate into society.

words.def: do something wrong and not be caught or punished
words.ex: With cameras everywhere, it’s hard to get away with street crime.

words.def: using someone else’s personal details, usually to get money
words.ex: Someone opened a credit card in my name — classic identity theft.

words.def: crime committed using the internet
words.ex: Online scams have become part of daily life.

words.def: video recorded by security cameras
words.ex: Police identified the robbers from CCTV footage.

words.def: crime planned and carried out by large criminal groups
words.ex: Organised crime controls much of the drug trade.

words.def: be caught in the act of doing something wrong
words.ex: He was caught red-handed taking money from the till.

words.w: go straight / keep your nose clean
words.def: stop committing crime and obey the law
words.ex: After two years behind bars, he decided to go straight.

words.def: be in prison
words.ex: He’s doing time for drink-driving.

words.def: a policy of punishing every offence, however small
words.ex: The city introduced zero tolerance for littering.

words.w: the full weight of the law
words.def: the most severe punishment possible
words.ex: Traffickers should face the full weight of the law.

words.def: the exact words of a law, with no flexibility
words.ex: He broke the letter of the law, but not its spirit.

words.def: someone with a long, settled habit of crime
words.ex: Prison can turn a first-time offender into a hardened criminal.

words.def: be influenced by others to behave badly
words.ex: He was a good kid who was led astray by older boys.

words.def: a young person who has committed a crime (formal: juvenile delinquent)
words.ex: Young offenders need guidance more than punishment.

words.def: non-violent crime by professionals, e.g. fraud or embezzlement
words.ex: White-collar crime is rarely punished as harshly as street crime.

words.def: secretly stealing money from the organisation you work for
words.ex: The accountant was jailed for embezzlement.

words.def: killing someone without intending to; murder is planned
words.ex: The careless driver was convicted of manslaughter, not murder.

words.w: be released on bail / be kept in custody
words.def: be freed before trial after paying money / be kept in prison before trial
words.ex: He was released on bail until his trial.

words.def: the deep reasons behind crime, such as poverty or unemployment
words.ex: Prisons don’t address the root causes of crime.

words.def: the issue is complicated; there is no simple answer
words.ex: It’s not black and white — it depends on the crime.

glossary.def: the process of judging a case in court
the official who decides a case / members of the public who decide the verdict
the final decision: guilty or not guilty
the person said to have broken the law
the lawyers who try to prove the defendant is guilty
information or objects that prove a crime (uncountable)
responsible for the crime / not responsible
release under conditions, e.g. good behaviour or an electronic tag
what you officially tell the police
(UK) lawyer in higher courts / lawyer who prepares legal documents
giving money to influence officials / dishonest behaviour by people in power
moving goods illegally across borders / moving drugs or people illegally for profit
physically attacking someone / attacking and robbing someone in public
taking someone by force and keeping them

mistakes.right: My phone was stolen. / I was robbed.
mistakes.why: Steal a thing; rob a person or place.

mistakes.wrong: There was a robbery in our empty flat.
mistakes.why: Burglary = breaking into a building; robbery involves force against a person.

mistakes.right: They found some evidence / a piece of evidence.

mistakes.wrong: He was accused, so he went to prison.
mistakes.right: He was convicted, so he went to prison.
Punishments should deter people. / act as a deterrent.
mistakes.why: Deter is the verb; deterrent is the noun.
Word stress changes how fluent you sound.

structure.note: Part 3 answers of 30–45 seconds follow this shape. You don’t need all five every time — but never stop after step 1.

openers: I’m in two minds about this.
It depends on which crimes we’re talking about.

part1.q: Is your neighbourhood generally safe, in your opinion?

model.6: Yes, I think my neighbourhood is quite safe. There is some **petty crime**, like **pickpocketing** in the bazaar, but I usually feel safe walking at night.
model.7: On the whole, yes. It’s a quiet residential area, so serious crime is rare. The main problem is **petty crime** — a neighbour had his phone snatched last year — but **the crime rate** is low compared to the city centre.
model.8: Generally speaking, yes — though “safe” is relative. Violent crime is almost unheard of, but **petty theft** is a different story; phone-snatching by motorbike has become a bit of a local plague. So I feel safe, just not careless.

part1.q: What would you do if you saw someone committing a petty crime?
part1.tip: It’s hypothetical — use would: “I’d probably…”, “I wouldn’t…”

model.6: I would probably call the police. I wouldn’t try to stop the person myself, because it could be dangerous.
model.7: I’d probably try to be a good **witness** rather than a hero — notice what the person looked like and **report it to the police**. Stepping in myself could easily make things worse.
model.8: Honestly, I’d like to think I’d intervene, but realistically I’d hold back and be a useful **witness** — get a description, maybe a photo, and **report it** straight away. A stolen wallet isn’t worth getting hurt for.

part1.q: Do you think people in your area are worried about drunk driving?

model.6: Not really. **Drink-driving** is not very common here, so people worry more about fast driving and accidents.
model.7: Not that much, to be honest. **Drink-driving** isn’t a big issue in my area, partly for cultural reasons. People are far more worried about speeding and drivers using their phones.
model.8: It’s not really on people’s radar. **Drink-driving** is relatively rare where I live, so the anxiety is directed elsewhere — reckless motorbikes and drivers glued to their phones are the real menace on our roads.

part1.q: Do you know anyone who works in law enforcement?

model.6: Yes, my cousin is a police officer. He says his job is hard but interesting.
model.7: Yes, actually — a cousin of mine works in **law enforcement**. He’s in the traffic police, so it’s less dramatic than it sounds; it’s mostly accidents and fines rather than chasing criminals.
model.8: I do, as it happens. A family friend is a detective, and what struck me is how unglamorous it is compared to crime dramas — mostly paperwork, **CCTV footage** and waiting, rather than car chases.

part1.q: Are online scams common where you live?

model.6: Yes, they are quite common. Many people get fake messages that ask for their bank card number.
model.7: Very common, unfortunately. Almost everyone I know has received a fake text pretending to be from a bank. **Cybercrime** is growing because it’s cheap and the **fraudsters** are hard to catch.
model.8: Sadly, yes — **online scams** have pretty much become part of daily life. My mother nearly fell for a fake parcel-delivery link last month. What makes it insidious is that **fraudsters** can operate from anywhere and rarely leave a trace.

part1.q: Do you enjoy crime films or TV series?

model.6: Yes, I like crime series. I enjoy trying to guess who the criminal is before the end.
model.7: I do, especially detective series. I like the puzzle element — piecing together the **evidence** and working out who **committed the crime** before the detective does.
model.8: I’m hooked on them, to be honest. A good crime drama is less about the crime than about motive — why an ordinary person **turns to crime**. That psychological side interests me more than the twist at the end.

part2.cue: Describe a crime you have heard about.
points: how you found out about it
part2.explain: and explain how it affected you or others.
phrases: It was reported to the police

model.6:
I’d like to talk about a crime that happened to my friend’s sister last winter. It was a **robbery** on Vali-Asr Street in Tehran, in the evening. She was walking home and talking on her phone. Suddenly, two men on a motorbike came very close, and one of them took the phone from her hand. Then they drove away very fast. She was shocked, but luckily she was not hurt.

I found out about it the same night, because my friend called me and told me the whole story. The next day they went to the police station and **reported the crime**. The police said this kind of crime is very common, and that it is difficult to catch the **robbers**.

This crime affected me a lot. Now I am more careful when I use my phone in the street. I don’t walk and talk on the phone near the road anymore. I think many people in my city changed their habits because of crimes like this.
model.7:
The crime I’d like to describe is a phone **robbery** that happened to a close friend’s sister last winter, on Vali-Asr Street in Tehran — one of the busiest streets in the city, which made it even more shocking.

It was early evening and she was walking home while chatting on her phone. All of a sudden, a motorbike with two men on it pulled up beside her, and the passenger snatched the phone right out of her hand. The whole thing took about three seconds. She wasn’t physically hurt, but she was badly shaken.

I heard about it that same night, when my friend called me, still quite upset. The next morning they **reported it to the police**, who were sympathetic but honest: this kind of **petty crime** is so widespread that unless there’s clear **CCTV footage**, the chances of catching the culprits are slim.

As for how it affected people, it changed our habits more than anything. My friend’s sister stopped using her phone on the street altogether, and I became much more aware of my surroundings. It also made me wonder whether stronger policing would **act as a deterrent**, or whether the real problem is young people with no jobs **turning to crime**.
model.8:
I’d like to talk about something that happened to a friend’s sister last winter — a motorbike phone-snatching on Vali-Asr Street. It’s a fairly common crime in Tehran, but hearing it from someone close made it feel very different from reading about it.

It happened at around six in the evening, right in the rush hour. She was walking home, phone pressed to her ear, when a motorbike mounted the pavement behind her. Before she’d even registered the noise, the passenger had snatched the phone and they’d disappeared into the traffic. Nobody around her had time to react.

I found out that night, when my friend rang me, half furious and half relieved that her sister hadn’t been dragged along the ground, which apparently happens. They **filed a report** the next day, and the officer was candid: unless there’s **CCTV footage** of the number plate, cases like this rarely go anywhere — most snatchers simply **get away with it**.

What struck me most was the impact. Materially, it was just a phone. But it took her weeks to feel comfortable on that street again, and it quietly rewired the rest of us — none of my friends takes a call on the pavement now. And it left me with a question I still can’t settle: whether these crimes call for being **tougher on crime**, or whether the answer lies in **the root causes** — unemployment, and young men with very few options **turning to crime**.

part3.q: Do you think strict punishments act as a deterrent to serious crimes like murder or drug trafficking? Why or why not?
chips: the full weight of the law

model.6: I think strict punishments help a little, but not completely. Some people are afraid of going to prison, so they don’t **commit crimes**. But people who commit very serious crimes often don’t think about the punishment.
model.7: To some extent, yes. **Harsh sentences** probably **act as a deterrent** for people who plan carefully, like drug traffickers, because they calculate the risk. But many murders happen in a moment of anger, and in that situation nobody thinks about the law. So I’d say the chance of getting caught matters more than how severe the punishment is.
model.8: **It’s not black and white.** For calculated crimes like drug trafficking, the threat of **the full weight of the law** may well shift the risk calculation. But criminologists generally find that what really **deters** people is the likelihood of being caught, not the severity of the sentence. And crimes of passion are, almost by definition, not rational — so no punishment, however harsh, is likely to prevent them.

part3.q: How can communities work together to reduce crime rates?

model.6: Neighbours can get to know each other and watch the street. They can also tell the police when they see something strange. Communities can also organise activities for young people.
model.7: I think the key is social connection. In areas where neighbours know each other, people notice strangers and **report** suspicious activity quickly. Local councils can also set up youth clubs and sports programmes, which keep teenagers busy and reduce the chance that they **turn to crime**.
model.8: Mostly by doing what the police can’t — being present. Neighbourhood watch schemes, well-lit streets and simply knowing who lives next door make a place far less attractive to criminals. Beyond that, investing in young people through mentoring, sport and apprenticeships tackles **the root causes of crime**, rather than just reacting to it.

part3.q: Do you think lenient sentences for petty crimes encourage reoffending? Why?

model.6: Maybe sometimes. If the punishment is very small, some people may do the same crime again. But prison is not always a good idea for small crimes.
model.7: Not necessarily. You could argue that **lenient sentences** send the message that crime pays, but sending petty offenders to prison often makes things worse — they mix with serious criminals and are more likely to **reoffend** when they’re released. **Community service** can be a better option.
model.8: **I’d actually argue the opposite.** Being **soft on crime** isn’t the issue so much as being smart about it. Prison is often a school for crime — a young shoplifter can come out a **hardened criminal**. **Non-custodial sentences** keep people connected to work and family, which is exactly what makes them less likely to **reoffend**.

part3.q: How effective do you think technology is in preventing or solving crimes?

model.6: I think it is very helpful. **CCTV** cameras help the police find criminals, and people are afraid to commit crimes when there are cameras.
model.7: It’s become extremely effective, especially for solving crimes. **CCTV footage**, digital fingerprints and phone data make it much easier to identify suspects, and cameras can also **act as a deterrent**. However, technology has also created new crimes, like **identity theft** and online scams.
model.8: **It’s a double-edged sword.** On the one hand, **CCTV**, facial recognition and digital forensics have transformed investigations — it’s far harder to **get away with** a street crime than it was twenty years ago. On the other hand, the same technology has opened up entirely new territory, and **cybercrime** tends to stay one step ahead of law enforcement. There’s also a privacy cost we don’t discuss enough.

part3.q: How do you think crimes in the future will differ from those today?

model.6: I think there will be more crime on the internet and less crime in the street. For example, people will steal money from bank accounts, not from pockets.
model.7: I expect **cybercrime** to keep growing while traditional street crime falls. As more of our lives move online, criminals will focus on **identity theft**, scams and hacking. AI might also make fraud more convincing, for example with fake voices.
model.8: I suspect crime will become increasingly invisible. The pickpocket is being replaced by the scammer who never leaves his bedroom — and with AI-generated voices, **fraud** is becoming disturbingly persuasive. **The irony is that** as our streets get safer, our digital lives may become the most dangerous neighbourhood we have.

part3.q: Do you believe criminals who serve time can successfully reintegrate back into society? Why or why not?

model.6: Yes, I think they can, but it is difficult. Many companies don’t want to hire someone with a **criminal record**. They need help to find a job.
model.7: Yes, as long as they get the right support. The biggest obstacle is a **criminal record**, which makes it very hard to find work. Without a job, people are much more likely to **reoffend**, so training and support after release are essential for them to **reintegrate into society**.
model.8: I believe many can, but the system often sets them up to fail. Someone leaves prison wanting to **go straight**, then discovers that a **criminal record** closes almost every door. If we want fewer repeat offenders, we have to offer a realistic path back — education inside prison, employers willing to give second chances — otherwise we’re just recycling people back into crime.

part3.q: Should young offenders be sent to prison?

model.6: I don’t think so. Young people can make mistakes, and prison can make them worse. **Community service** is a better punishment for them.
model.7: In most cases, no. Teenagers who **commit a crime** have often been **led astray** by older friends. Prison exposes them to serious criminals, so they’re likely to **reoffend**. A **non-custodial sentence**, like community service, teaches responsibility without destroying their future.
model.8: Only as a last resort. A **young offender** needs to understand that they’ve slipped up, but locking them up risks turning a mistake into a career — they come out with new contacts and a **criminal record**. Short of serious violence, community service or probation seems far more likely to help them **keep their nose clean** in the long run.

part3.q: Is the crime rate lower nowadays than in the past?

model.6: I think some crimes are lower, like **burglary**, because houses have better security. But crime on the internet is higher now.
model.7: **It depends on which crimes we’re talking about.** Property crimes like **burglary** have fallen in many cities because of better home security and **CCTV**. But **cybercrime** has grown enormously, so overall it’s hard to say that crime is lower.
model.8: **I’m in two minds about it.** Statistically, many traditional crimes such as burglary and car theft have dropped sharply. But I’m not sure the numbers tell the whole story — online **fraud** is massively under-reported, so crime may not have fallen so much as moved somewhere harder to measure.

easy.prompt: Someone who steals from a shop is a ______.
easy.explain: Shoplifter = shop. A pickpocket steals from pockets and bags.

easy.prompt: Young people who spray paint on bus stops are guilty of ______.
While we were on holiday, someone broke into our flat — it was a ______.
easy.explain: Breaking into a building (often empty) = burglary.

easy.prompt: My phone was ______ on the metro.
easy.explain: You steal a thing; you rob a person or place.

easy.prompt: She saw the whole thing, so the police asked her to be a ______.
easy.explain: A witness is someone who saw what happened.

easy.prompt: He lost his licence for ______ — he was three times over the limit.
The police ______ the man outside the bank.
easy.explain: The police arrest; a court convicts and sentences.

easy.prompt: Most people who ______ a crime never expect to be caught.
easy.explain: The fixed collocation is commit a crime.

easy.prompt: ______ in our city has fallen by 10% this year.
easy.explain: The crime rate = how much crime there is.

easy.prompt: It’s hard to get a job if you have a ______.
easy.explain: A criminal record lists the crimes you were convicted of.

medium.prompt: Without job training, many ex-prisoners ______ within a year.
medium.explain: reoffend = commit a crime again after being punished. ‘Rehabilitation’ is a noun — the sentence needs a verb.

medium.prompt: Many people believe CCTV cameras ______ to thieves.
medium.explain: Something that stops people committing crime acts as a deterrent.

medium.prompt: Just a small fine for such a serious offence? That’s a very ______ sentence.
medium.explain: Lenient = lighter than expected. Harsh is the opposite.

medium.prompt: Politicians often promise to be ______ on crime before an election.
medium.explain: The fixed phrase is be tough on crime (opposite: soft on crime).

medium.prompt: Instead of prison, she was ordered to do 200 hours of ______.
medium.explain: Community service is a non-custodial sentence.

medium.prompt: Poverty is one reason why some young people ______.
medium.explain: turn to crime = start committing crimes.

medium.prompt: Someone opened a credit card in my name — I’m a victim of ______.
medium.explain: Using your personal details = identity theft.

medium.prompt: He was ______ of fraud and sentenced to three years.
medium.explain: Convicted = found guilty by a court. Accused only means suspected.

medium.prompt: The police identified the robbers from ______.
medium.explain: CCTV footage = video from security cameras.

medium.prompt: Former prisoners need support to ______ into society.
medium.explain: reintegrate into society = return to normal life.

strong.prompt: He was caught ______ taking money from the till.
strong.explain: caught red-handed = caught in the act.

strong.prompt: After five years behind bars, he decided to ______ and found a job.
The school has a ______ policy on bullying: even one incident means suspension.
strong.explain: Zero tolerance = every offence is punished, however small.

strong.prompt: Stealing bread to feed your children breaks ______, but perhaps not its spirit.
options: the full weight of the law
strong.explain: The letter of the law = its exact words, with no flexibility.

strong.prompt: She killed a cyclist by driving carelessly. She didn’t intend to, so she was convicted of ______, not murder.
strong.explain: Manslaughter = killing without intent. Murder is planned.

strong.prompt: The accountant had been quietly moving company money into his own account for years — a classic case of ______.
strong.explain: Embezzlement = stealing from the organisation you work for.

strong.prompt: Fraud, embezzlement and insider trading are examples of ______ crime.
strong.explain: White-collar crime = non-violent crime by professionals.

strong.prompt: Critics argue that prison can turn a first-time offender into a ______ criminal.
strong.explain: A hardened criminal has a long, settled habit of crime.

strong.prompt: He was a good kid, but he was ______ by older boys in the neighbourhood.
strong.explain: be led astray = be influenced by others to behave badly.

strong.prompt: While waiting for his trial, he was released on ______.
strong.explain: Released on bail = freed before trial after paying money.

sourceNotes: Source PDF and DOCX are the same handout; both say “7 questions” in Part 3 but list 6 — two were added here (p3-7, p3-8), built on the handout’s own phrase sections.
Part 1 had 4 questions; p1-5 and p1-6 were added to reach 6.
Fixed typos: Extorsion → Extortion; “It’s not back and white” → black and white.
Exercise 3 in the handout is missing the blank for “act as a deterrent”; its content is covered in the Medium test instead.
Courtroom and serious-crime terms moved to a recognise-only glossary: useful for reading, rarely needed in Speaking.
